item.title: Tartine Bakery soft opens at Strawberry Village; official opening Aug. 19
item.description: Staff training is underway at the new Tartine Bakery in Strawberry Village, which has been open intermittently since Aug. 13. The formal opening is set for Aug. 19.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon Peninsula residents no longer have to drive to San Francisco, or wait in its hourlong lines, for a Tartine country loaf.

The bakery will formally open its first North Bay store Aug. 19 at the Strawberry Village shopping center, filling two storefronts that had sat empty for years and ending a wait that began when Tartine announced the location in March 2025.

The 3,091-square-foot bakery and cafe sits in the same cluster as Safeway, Calico Corners and High Tech Burrito. It will be open 8 a.m.-4 p.m. daily and will sell the sourdough, morning buns and pastries that built the brand, soft-scramble tartines and breakfast sandwiches on a sweet potato bun, along with lunch items including ham-and-gruyere sandwiches and a double smash burger with American cheese, celery remoulade and fennel confit.

Tartine began opening intermittently for staff trainings on Aug. 13, with staff saying a friends and family soft opening was set for Aug. 15 and Aug. 16 and the public soft opening would begin Aug. 17.

San Francisco firm Studio BBA designed the space to pick up the shopping center’s Mediterranean look, with high ceilings, an open floor plan and sightlines that let customers watch the bakers work.

The store is also a return to the peninsula’s doorstep for a business that started nearby. Founders Chad Robertson and Elisabeth Prueitt honed their craft at Bay Village Breads in Point Reyes Station, then moved to 17 Madrona St. in Mill Valley in 2000. They left for San Francisco in 2002 and opened the first Tartine at 18th and Guerrero streets in the Mission district, where customers reserved bread three days ahead and lined up each morning for the afternoon bake.

The pair won the James Beard Foundation award for the best pastry chefs in America in 2008, and Bon Appétit magazine called Tartine “America’s most influential bakery” in 2017. Robertson’s 2010 book, “Tartine Bread,” helped set off the home sourdough boom.

Tartine’s three other Bay Area locations are all in San Francisco: the original Mission bakery, the Tartine Manufactory and a store in the Inner Sunset. The company also runs seven locations in Los Angeles and six in Seoul, South Korea, and has leased a former CVS in San Francisco’s Financial District, a fourth city store it expects to open next year.

item.title: Tiburon to spend $250k to dig out of audit backlog
item.description: Tiburon will spend up to $250,000 on outside accountants to clear a three-year backlog of unfinished financial audits.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon will spend up to $250,000 on outside accountants to clear a three-year backlog of unfinished financial audits, work that isn’t expected to leave the town current until the middle of 2027 at the earliest.

The Town Council voted 4-0 on Aug. 5 to approve a $195,000 contract with Rogers Anderson Malody & Scott, a San Bernardino accounting firm known as RAMS, to help finish audits for fiscal years 2023-2024, 2024-2025 and 2025-2026. Councilmember Holli Thier, who attended by videoconference, was no longer on the call when the vote was taken.

It is the second agreement the town has signed with the firm. Town Manager Greg Chanis approved an initial $55,000 contract in July under his own signing authority, below the amount that requires council approval. Neither needed a budget amendment, because the current fiscal year 2026-2027 budget already carried money for the work. That money had been going to Regional Government Services, which had provided the town’s finance and accounting help until Tiburon dropped it in July. Chanis said after the meeting that ending that contract cost the town nothing.

The oldest audit, covering fiscal 2024, is scheduled to begin Aug. 17, with financial statements presented to the council by the end of October, Chanis said. The fiscal 2025 audit is projected for January to March 2027, and fiscal 2026, the year that ended June 30, for April to June 2027. The town would be caught up by late July 2027 at the latest.

Much of the delay is a scheduling problem. September through December is the busy season for municipal audits and firms are typically booked solid, Chanis said, adding that the town would keep looking for chances to shorten the turnaround. The town’s auditor, The Pun Group of Santa Ana, works alongside RAMS for several other government agencies, a relationship Chanis credited with securing the Aug. 17 start date quickly. He said The Pun Group has also put Tiburon at the top of its list for any opening.

“If their schedule changes or if one of their current customers drops out, and there’s — a slot opens up, we’d be able to move faster on the subsequent audits,” Chanis said.

The $195,000 buys more than audit help. Under the firm’s proposal, it also covers writing standard operating procedures, reviewing internal-control problems The Pun Group flagged in fiscal years 2021-2022 through 2023-2024, auditing who has access to the town’s financial software and cross-training staff.<...

item.title: Belvedere finds shoreline building it never approved
item.description: Belvedere planning officials walking the shoreline at low tide in March found a two-story building on Beach Road the city says it never approved.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere planning officials walking the shoreline at low tide in March found a two-story building standing at the water’s edge on Beach Road that the city says it never approved. More than four months later, the owner still hasn’t responded.

Building Inspector Genaro Muniz posted a stop-work order on the exterior of the main house at 344 Beach Road on March 25. It says work on the structure was found “not to comply or to be deficient” for a single reason: “For building an illegal structure without Planning or Building Dept. approval.”

The city then obtained photographs from a resident that appear to document the sequence. Images taken in August and September 2024 show the shoreline below the main house with no second building on it. Photos from February 2025 show a two-story structure under construction, sheathed in housewrap with its windows set and scaffolding along one side. Photos taken March 23 show the same building finished — flat-roofed, painted and glassed in on two floors, its lower wall rising from the stone seawall a few feet above the tideline.

Planning and Building Director Rebecca Markwick Markwick said basic details — height, square footage and how the building is being used — remain unknown because the site can’t be seen from Beach Road and the owner has not discussed the work with the city.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: In 2024 (left), the seawall below the main house at 344 Beach Road held no second structure beside the property’s dock. By this March (right), a flat-roofed two-story building stood in that spot, painted and glassed in on both floors. Belvedere posted a stop-work order on the main house March 25 over what it called an illegal structure built without planning or building approval. The owner has not responded to the city. (via city of Belvedere)

item.title: ‘Birdhouse,’ basket swings in mix for Cypress Hollow Park
item.description: Basket swings, a birdhouse climbing structure and wooden towers with slides are among options Tiburon is weighing for a rebuilt Cypress Hollow playground.
item.content:encoded:
Tire and basket swings, a climbing structure shaped like a birdhouse and wooden play towers with slides are among the options Tiburon is weighing for a rebuilt playground at Cypress Hollow Park.

Members of the Tiburon Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission’s mini-parks subcommittee presented preliminary concepts from three playground-equipment vendors at an in-person workshop July 28 and a virtual workshop Aug. 4.

The designs and the feedback on them will be folded into the 60%-completed design set that Santa Rosa-based park designer Carlile Macy is preparing for the commission’s special meeting at 6 p.m. Aug. 24, subcommittee member and parks Commissioner Chuck Hornbrook said during the Aug. 4 session.

Hornbrook said structures can be mixed and matched across manufacturers for the park’s new play area of roughly 3,000 square feet, a 50% increase over the 2,000 square feet of play space at the half-acre park now.

Even with the expansion, Hornbrook said, the park’s size limits which marquee structures will fit. He said the Bel Aire play area covers 0.7 acres and South of the Knoll Park about 6.5 acres.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: A rendering from Earthscape Play shows a basket swing among preliminary options for a rebuilt playground at Cypress Hollow Park. The Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission’s mini-parks subcommittee presented concepts from three vendors at workshops July 28 and Aug. 4. No design has been chosen, and no construction has been approved.

item.title: Tiburon real-estate broker turned rocker releases his third album
item.description: Dan Mihalovich spent his teens at The Fillmore. Now the Tiburon commercial real-estate broker has released his third album under the name Dan Moss.
item.content:encoded:
Dan Mihalovich spent his formative teen years at The Fillmore in San Francisco, drawing inspiration from the rock legends who took the stage and immersing himself in the venue’s counterculture vibe.

“I think I’m always looking for that kind of electrifying connection, if you can find it, with bands or music,” Mihal­ovich says.

Inspired by acts like Janis Joplin, Jimi Hendrix and The Beatles, Mihalovich picked up a guitar at age 12 and dreamed of a life in rock ’n’ roll.

While he established his career in commercial real estate, music remained a lifelong hobby — until about six years ago, when Mihalovich decided he wanted to turn his passion into a second career. Music, he says, uses a different part of his brain.

“I think a lot of what we do in our daily lives suppresses that kind of brain activity,” he says. “After working in the commercial real estate for so long, I got to a point where I just didn’t love doing it anymore. And I thought that, all of that brain activity is really interfering with what I really want to do.”

He’s since released three albums under his stage name, Dan Moss. The most recent, “Blueberry Blonde,” was released in July on Spotify and Apple Music and on vinyl.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Tiburon resident Dan Mihalovich holds his custom Gibson Les Paul Aug. 4 at The Boardwalk shopping center, wearing a shirt bearing the cover art from his third album, ‘Blueberry Blonde.’ He released the album in July under the name Dan Moss and will play a release party Oct. 23 at Peri’s Tavern in Fairfax. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Tiburon council sends home expansion back for design review
item.description: Three neighbors appealed the approval, saying the 794-square-foot addition would block their views and that the board never seriously weighed building down.
item.content:encoded:
The Tiburon Town Council has sent a Hawthorne Terrace couple’s home expansion back to the Design Review Board, ordering a closer look at whether the project can be built lower to spare neighbors’ views.

The council voted 3-1 on Aug. 5 to return the proposed 794-square-foot expansion at 700 Hawthorne Drive to the board, instructing it to scrutinize alternatives to the height increase and to gather better visual evidence of how neighbors would be affected.

The move came after the council heard separate appeals from three neighbors: Kamran Shirazi of 3 Rock Hill Road, Ryan Lee of 699 Hawthorne Drive and Neda Shafaghi of 705 Hawthorne Drive. They sought to overturn the design board’s approval of the plans submitted by homeowners Eric Tiret and Caely Cusick.

Councilmember Holli Thier cast the opposing vote, saying she felt neighbor sentiment was substantial enough to fully grant the neighbors’ appeals and overturn the project approval. Councilmember Jack Ryan recused himself because he owns property within 500 feet of Cusick and Tiret’s home.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: The view from 699 Hawthorne Drive looks across the roofline of 700 Hawthorne Drive toward Richardson Bay and Sausalito. Ryan Lee, one of three neighbors who appealed, said the proposed addition would cut into the sight line from his great room. The Town Council on Aug. 5 sent the project back to the Design Review Board, which had approved it in April on conditions that included removing the red-leafed photinia shrub at center right. (Ryan Lee via town of Tiburon)

item.title: New Business: Marin Service Course opens new bike shop at The Boardwalk
item.description: Marin Service Course, owned by Tiburon's Peter Lucas, has opened a second location at The Boardwalk.
item.content:encoded:
While growing up on Centro West Street, Peter Lucas would turn his daily bike ride to Del Mar Middle School into an adventure.

He says he used to “bomb down the hill” that descends from Old St. Hilary’s Landmark. Then it was time for tricks.

“I would try and wheelie the whole way to Del Mar school,” he says.

Lucas’ love for biking hasn’t waned, and now the Tiburon resident is aiming to share his passion with the community. Lucas openedMarin Service Courseat The Boardwalk shopping center July 25. It’s the business’s second location, following the original Fairfax shop that opened in 2019. The Tiburon outpost replaces Diana’s of Tiburon, the gift shop that closed in April 2025 after owner Diana Maureen decided to retire.

Marin Service Course sells and services bikes and stocks nutrition products for cyclists, and it offers bike fitting, coaching and organized community rides.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Peter Lucas opened Marin Service Course at The Boardwalk shopping center July 25, the second location for the bike shop he founded in Fairfax in 2019. Lucas, who grew up on Centro West Street riding to Del Mar Middle School, built the store around a bar, at rear, where customers can drink free espresso and watch races. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A passion for Italy inspires chocolatier’s small-batch bonbons
item.description: John Cruger makes small-batch Italian-inspired bonbons in Tiburon and sells them at one place: the Paradise Coffee cart at Point Tiburon Plaza.
item.content:encoded:
John Cruger is the man behind a selection of sweet treats that can be found only on Tiburon Boulevard.

At Paradise Coffee, the mobile coffee cart at Point Tiburon Plaza, customers can buy items from Cruger’s small-batch chocolate line, which he calls Gio Dolce. There are bonbons with flavors like Aperol, espresso martini and cinnamon, as well as what Cruger calls his masterpiece: a “cafe mocha” chocolate shaped like a tiny Starbucks cup with three layers — dark chocolate, caramel chocolate and white chocolate cheesecake — all held together with a swirl of espresso syrup.

“The bonbons are real shiny, kind of like pearls,” he says while walking his dog along Shoreline Park Aug. 7. “And they’re all Italian inspired and they’re all inspired by the Amalfi Coast.”

Cruger, 61, makes the bonbons himself in Tiburon, buying chocolate from Switzerland and cocoa butter from the United Kingdom, then using ingredients sourced from Northern California for the fillings and flavorings. The result is a small-batch operation shaped by the climate as much as the recipe.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: John Cruger, seen here Aug. 7 walking his dog in Shoreline Park, produces small-batch chocolates sold exclusively at Paradise Coffee, the mobile coffee cart at Point Tiburon Plaza. (Tyler Callister / The Ark)

item.title: Jean Barnett
item.description: Jean Barnett, age 94, passed away in Santa Rosa on July 12, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Jean Barnett, age 94, passed away in Santa Rosa on July 12, 2026, after a brief illness following a long battle with dementia.

Jean was preceded in death by her beloved husband, James Barnett, with whom she shared 63 years of marriage before his passing in 2020. Together they built a life centered on family, friendship, and a love of the outdoors.

Born and raised in Sebastopol and educated at Stanford, Jean spent her adult years in Marin County, where she devoted herself to raising her family and embracing the natural beauty of California. She found joy in nature, travel, golf, gardening, and watercolor painting, pursuits that reflected her curiosity, creativity, and appreciation for the world around her.

Jean was known for her warmth and generosity of spirit. She always had a friendly smile and a kind word to share, and her genuine interest in others made her a lifelong friend to many. Her quiet kindness and gracious presence touched countless lives and will be remembered by all who knew her.

She is survived by her sister Doreen, sons Charlie and Michael, and her grandchildren, Kyle and Nora, who will cherish her memory and carry forward the values of kindness, friendship, and appreciation for life’s simple pleasures that she embodied so well.

Jean’s family takes comfort in the many wonderful memories she leaves behind and in the lasting impact she had on the lives of those fortunate enough to know and love her.
item.dc:creator: Reader submitted

item.title: A Life Well Lived: Norman Allen Spencer
item.description: Norman Allen Spencer passed away peacefully at his home in Tiburon, California, on July 20, 2026, at the age of 83.
item.content:encoded:
Norman Allen Spencer passed away peacefully at his home in Tiburon, California, on July 20, 2026, at the age of 83. While his family grieves his loss, they celebrate a life that was rich in love, friendship, and purpose.

Born on August 5, 1942, in Seattle, Washington, to Henry Norman Spencer and Mary Elva Dillingham Spencer, Norm grew up in the Pacific Northwest. He graduated from Roosevelt High School before earning his degree from the University of Washington in 1964.

In 1968, Norm met Sally Kolthoff in San Francisco, where they married in 1974 before moving to Tiburon in 1975. Together they shared 52 wonderful years of marriage, raising a family, traveling, and enjoying life together.

Norm enjoyed an extraordinary 41-year career in commercial real estate — a profession he loved and often said he never considered “work.” He began at Coldwell Banker, where he introduced Hines to the opportunity that became the iconic 101 California St. It marked the beginning of his distinguished career with Hines, where he spent more than 25 years as an executive in the San Francisco office.

At Hines, Norm was known not only for his expertise and professionalism, but also for his integrity, warmth, and ability to build lasting relationships. He retired in 2010 after contributing to many renowned office buildings throughout Northern and Southern California. To Norm, however, the greatest reward of his career was never the buildings themselves — it was the friendships he made along the way.

At the height of his commercial real-estate career, Norm pursued his interest in viticulture at UC Davis, inspired by his growing passion for wine. This led to the creation of Spencer Vineyards in Oakville, where they built a family home that became the backdrop for more than three decades of family dinners, milestone celebrations, summer weekends, and treasured traditions.

Outside the office, Norm embraced life with enthusiasm. Golf was one of his greatest joys, but not because of the score. As a proud member of Meadow Club, Kohanaiki, Summit Muni, and formerly the Olympic Club and Silverado, he treasured the camaraderie, the opportunity to win a few dollars, and the friendships forged over 18 holes. His favorite course was never defined by its scenery — it was wherever he happened to be playing with his buddies, his son Greg, or his grandson Spencer.

item.title: Marin artists pay tribute to the spirit of America in ‘We the People’
item.description: Eight local artists are showing work at Tiburon Town Hall in "We the People," an exhibit marking the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence.
item.content:encoded:
Eight local artists are featured in “We the People,” a Tiburon Town Hall exhibition designed to celebrate the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence.

The exhibit, sponsored by the Heritage & Arts Commission, runs through Aug. 31 in Town Hall’s downstairs gallery. The commission put out an open call earlier this summer inviting peninsula residents of all ages to submit works across all mediums that “explore historical events, cultural traditions, landscapes, everyday life, national symbols or personal narratives that speak to the spirit of America.”
item.dc:creator: Diane Smith
item.media:description: ‘Stand Up for Democracy!’ is a mixed-media piece by Jeri Brittell of Tiburon, on display through Aug. 31 in the downstairs gallery at Tiburon Town Hall as part of ‘We the People.’ The exhibition features work by eight local artists marking the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence. (via Jeri Brittell)

item.title: Filing deadline extends as Tiburon councilmember won’t seek third term; Belvedere draws late challenge
item.description: Nine of the 12 races on Tiburon Peninsula ballots are now set. Seven candidates are running for three Tam Union school board seats, the most crowded contest.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon Mayor Jon Welner is not seeking a third term in the Nov. 3 election, assuring the Town Council of at least one new member, and in Belvedere a first-time candidate filed hours before the deadline to challenge both incumbents.

The Aug. 7 deadline settled nine of the 12 contests on Tiburon Peninsula ballots.

The Tiburon council, the Reed Union School District and the Tamalpais Union High School District stay open until 5 p.m. Aug. 12 because an incumbent in each did not file.

Welner took out nomination papers July 28 but did not return them before the 5 p.m. Aug. 7 deadline, leaving him off the ballot. Because a sitting officeholder did not file, the nomination period extended five days for everyone but incumbents.

Welner, who joined the council in 2018 after serving on the Planning Commission, said the town was better off than when he arrived. “It has been my great honor and privilege to serve the town of Tiburon over the last 16 years, first as a planning commissioner, then as a councilmember and finally as mayor,” he said.

He pointed to the town’s climate action plan and its sustainability element, which he said was the first in a California general plan. He also cited the acquisition of the Martha property, the purchase of the former sanitation pond next to McKegney Green, a master plan for the town’s parks and a traffic study of Tiburon Boulevard.

“All in all, we have left the town of Tiburon in better shape than we found it,” he said. “That’s a legacy to be proud of.”

Four candidates qualified for three seats. Incumbents Alice Fredericks and Jack Ryan filed and qualified July 29. Challenger Chuck Hornbrook, a member of the town’s Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission, qualified July 31. Faris Jafar, founder of a wealth-management firm, qualified Aug. 3.

Fredericks, first elected in 2001, is seeking an unprecedented seventh term.

With Welner out, two potential returning challengers pulled papers Aug. 10: Andrew Thompson, a former mayor and councilmember from 1992 to 2003, and Kathleen Defever, a planning commissioner since 2018. Neither had filed.

In Belvedere, Kate Benediktsson took out papers Aug. 6 and filed Aug. 7, challenging incumbents Peter Mark and Jane Cooper for two seats. As of Aug. 10, the city had not yet listed her as qualified.

item.title: Neighbors sue Marin County over housing project at Strawberry seminary site
item.description: The suit argues the county improperly waived the Strawberry Community Plan's ban on housing atop Chapel Hill, and that its environmental review fell short.
item.content:encoded:
A Strawberry neighbors’ group is suing Marin County to overturn its approval of a project that would remake the former Golden Gate Baptist Theological Seminary site into hundreds of homes, a senior-care facility and a graduate school.

Strawberry Residents for Sensible Development filed suit July 6 in Marin Superior Court. North Coast Land Holdings, the project’s developer, is named in the case as a real party in interest, meaning it can also defend the project in court. The litigation could delay a project that has drawn public debate for more than a decade.

On June 9, the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to approve North Coast’s plan for the hilltop site. The hearing drew about two dozen public speakers, most of them critical.

North Coast has worked through years of negotiations since buying the site in 2014, including a March 1 settlement with the Seminary Neighborhood Association, which agreed to drop its opposition to the project. But other Strawberry residents say the association represents only a small group and doesn’t speak for those who still object to the project.

The new resident group is part of that continued opposition. Its founder said a July 28 community meeting drew at least 30 residents. The group contends the approved project violates the Strawberry Community Plan and state environmental law.

The lawsuit makes two broad legal claims, both centered on Chapel Hill. North Coast plans 40 market-rate homes there, a mix of one- to four-bedroom units.

First, the lawsuit argues the county improperly waived the Strawberry Community Plan’s ban on housing atop Chapel Hill under state density-bonus law. The county’s own environmental review had found that an alternative design, which would meet the same density without the waiver, was environmentally superior. The lawsuit says the Board of Supervisors rejected that alternative without giving any reasoning.

Second, the lawsuit argues the environmental review required under the California Environmental Quality Act fell short. It says the review did not adequately assess the visual impact of developing Chapel Hill, including the loss of bay views; the raising of the athletic field with 220,000 cubic yards of excavated soil; the displacement of low-income residents whose homes would be demolished; or the county’s reliance on a 1953 permit that allowed up to 1,000 students on the site.

Attorney Michael Graf represents the group. The lawsuit...

item.title: Underwater robot to chart Richardson Bay's eelgrass meadows
item.description: So far the project only maps and monitors. The agency hopes to fund robotic planting next, with a $1.9 million grant.
item.content:encoded:
Like the shark it’s named for, Mako will cruise silently along the floor of Richardson Bay, hunting. But this predator is a robot, and what it’s hunting is eelgrass — the waving undersea meadows that are vital to the bay’s ecology.

Starting this month, the Richardson Bay Regional Agency will use an underwater drone to map and monitor Richardson Bay eelgrass beds. The bay agency has enlisted San Francisco-based Ulysses Ecosystem Engineering to study eelgrass beds using an autonomous underwater vehicle named Mako.

A $250,000 grant from the Marin Community Foundation will fund the project, a one-year award running through June 30, 2027.

Eelgrass is an ecological scaffold for marine life, home to a host of invertebrates and a preferred spawning ground for herring. Studies have shown it buffers wave action, improves water quality and sequesters carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Richardson Bay’s eelgrass beds are the second largest in San Francisco Bay and among the largest on the West Coast. Eelgrass, however, is in retreat worldwide because of shoreline development and pollution.
item.dc:creator: Gretchen Lang
item.media:description: Mako, Ulysses Ecosystem Engineering’s autonomous underwater drone, passes over a seagrass meadow off Perth, Australia. The Richardson Bay Regional Agency will use the drone starting this month to map and monitor eelgrass beds in the bay. (via Ulysses)

item.title: Tiburon promotes officer as Police Department adds fifth sergeant
item.description: Tiburon has added a fifth police sergeant and cut an officer position, promoting Justin Hettich, who had covered supervisor shifts since January 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon has added a fifth police sergeant position and reduced its authorized patrol officers by one, promoting an officer who had covered supervisor shifts since January 2025.

Justin Hettich’s promotion took effect July 1. The department announced it in a July 27 Instagram post, saying he has worked in law enforcement for more than 18 years, six of them in Tiburon.

The promotion leaves the department with five sergeants and six officers, along with four reserve officers, Police Chief Michelle Jean said. One of the six, Officer William Forrest Condit, has been on paid administrative leave since October, leaving five officers available for patrol. One of the five sergeants, Rob Law, works full time as a detective.

The supervisory opening dates to January 2025, when Law moved to detective duties under a six-month pilot program. Jean said that shift left a patrol team without a supervising sergeant and that Hettich has served as officer in charge since that month.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: Justin Hettich was promoted to Tiburon police sergeant effective July 1, filling a fifth sergeant position the town added in its new budget. Hettich joined the department in 2020 and had covered supervisor shifts as officer in charge since January 2025. (via Tiburon Police Department)

item.title: Consultant says proposed wall would worsen flooding in Tiburon's Bel Aire neighborhood
item.description: A consultant is advising against a proposed flood wall on one of the creeks that floods Tiburon's Bel Aire neighborhood, saying it would push water onto homes that don't flood now.
item.content:encoded:
The consultant designing a restoration project for two creeks that flood Tiburon’s Bel Aire neighborhood in heavy rain is advising against a proposed flood wall on one of them. The wall would push flooding into parts of the neighborhood that don’t flood now, the firm’s modeling found.

Officials delivered that update and detailed how work will proceed on the East and West creeks project during the July 28 Marin Flood Control District Zone 4 advisory board meeting, which featured only informational items and no votes.

The board also heard updates on a planned study addressing chronic flooding near Greenwood Cove Drive and a potential study evaluating levees near Strawberry Circle following tidal flooding in January.

The zone covers Tiburon’s Bel Aire neighborhood, parts of unincorporated Tiburon along Greenwood Cove Drive and homes along Strawberry Circle.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Verdantas hydrologist Janice Weldon showcases inundation modeling along the lower West Creek during a 50-year storm, or a storm with a 2% chance of occurring in a given year, during the Marin Flood Control District Zone 4 advisory board meeting July 28 at Westminster Presbyterian Church. The inundation projection does not account for pumping from the Cecilia Way and Cove pump stations. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Socal man sues Tiburon, Marin, PG&E over trip-and-fall
item.description: An Orange County man is suing Tiburon, Marin County and PG&E, saying a steel utility vault cover in the downtown sidewalk shifted under his weight and dropped him to the pavement.
item.content:encoded:
A Southern California man says a steel utility-vault cover embedded in the sidewalk in downtown Tiburon shifted under his weight and dropped him to the pavement, and he is suing the town, Marin County and Pacific Gas and Electric Co. over the injuries.

Daniel Byun, 55, of Orange County filed the complaint July 10 in Marin County Superior Court. It alleges the town and county created “an unreasonably dangerous condition” by failing to maintain the sidewalk near Fountain Plaza downtown, and that PG&E, as owner of the vault and its cover, failed to inspect and maintain the cover.

Byun first filed a claim against the town and county on or about Dec. 15, 2025, the complaint says. The county and town each rejected it the next month, clearing the way for the suit.

The complaint does not name a dollar figure. It says only that the damages exceed $35,000, the minimum for an unlimited civil case, and asks a jury to set the amount at trial.

Saul Wolf, one of Byun’s attorneys at Costa Mesa-based Easton & Easton LLP, told The Ark in a July 29 interview that the fall left Byun with fractured ribs, shoulder sprains, a torn biceps, a damaged knee and neck and back pain.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: DA declines to charge Tiburon man in alleged kidnapping of girlfriend
item.description: The Marin County District Attorney's Office has declined to file charges against an 18-year-old Tiburon man arrested in June on suspicion of kidnapping and robbing his girlfriend.
item.content:encoded:
The Marin County District Attorney’s Office has declined to file criminal charges against an 18-year-old Tiburon man who was arrested in June on suspicion of kidnapping and robbing his 17-year-old girlfriend.

The man surrendered at the Tiburon police station with his attorney June 16 and was booked into Marin County Jail on suspicion of kidnapping, robbery, child cruelty and false imprisonment. He was released the same day. Because prosecutors filed no charges, The Ark is not naming him under a policy of generally not identifying suspects before they are formally charged.

Police said the case stemmed from an argument shortly after 2 a.m. June 15, while the couple sat in a parked car near Heathcliff Drive. The man then began driving, and the girl tried to get out, but he put the car in reverse and accelerated with her door still open, police said. She tried to call 911, and he took her phone. The car stopped on Avenida Miraflores, near Del Mar Middle School, where she got out.

The girl ran to a nearby home and knocked, but no one answered, police said. She then walked alone to the police station to report what happened.

In the meantime, the man had gone to her father’s home in Mill Valley to say the girl had fled the car, police said. He returned her phone to the father, and the two men drove back toward Avenida Miraflores to look for her. Her father called police to report her missing, and officers were treating it as a missing-juvenile case when they arrived.

Police said the allegations of force and restraint came from the girl’s account to officers at the station.

A cite hearing, or pre-arraignment appearance, had been scheduled for July 28. The district attorney’s office confirmed July 30 that it did not file a criminal complaint.

item.title: Third owner wins Belvedere's approval for hillside home project
item.description: It's the same design the commission approved nine years ago. The architect called it "the exact design that was approved in June of 2017," apart from an outdoor inclined lift.
item.content:encoded:
Three owners have won Belvedere’s approval to build a mansion at 135 Belvedere Ave. since 2017. The first two sold the lot instead, the second at a $1.7 million loss, leaving a derelict 1957 house and a hillside of collapsing Monterey pines.

On July 21, the Planning Commission approved the third try — an 11,223-square-foot contemporary home more than twice the size zoning allows, and the same design it approved nine years ago.

The commission voted 4-0 to grant design review, a demolition permit and an exception to the city’s floor-area cap for architect David Kotzebue’s design, and to recommend City Council approval of a revocable license for private improvements in the city’s right of way.

The new home would replace a 3,764-square-foot residence on a steeply sloped, 52,965-square-foot lot overlooking Richardson Bay.

item.title: New Business: Club Pilates adds to fitness scene at Strawberry Village
item.description: Club Pilates has opened at Strawberry Village, joining a cluster of fitness businesses that already includes Pure Barre, Orangetheory, StretchLab and Hot Yoga Republic.
item.content:encoded:
Club Pilates opened June 25 in the Strawberry Village shopping center. The studio sits between Hot Yoga Republic and the recently opened Hydration Room. Club Pilates is the world’s largest Pilates brand, with more than 1,400 studios worldwide. The company operates more than 1,000 studios in North America and has expanded to 12 countries. Other Marin locations include Greenbrae, Novato and San Rafael.

Club Pilates offers classes seven days a week, focused on the Pilates “reformer,” a bed-like frame with a sliding carriage, adjustable springs for resistance, ropes, pulleys and a foot bar. The method was created by Joseph Pilates, a German-born fitness pioneer who overcame childhood illnesses by taking up gymnastics, boxing and yoga. The method emphasizes mindful breathing, precise movement and control.

“It’s not just about flexibility, which is kind of the misconception,” general manager Emma Roberts says. “You don’t have to be flexible to take Pilates. It can help you with your flexibility, but overall, it’s a low-impact form of exercise that just helps you continue to be active without hurting yourself.”
